newsitem.title: USA: Anti-smoking group calls for hearings on tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Anti-smoking group calls for hearings on tobacco.

text.p: An anti-smoking group Monday called for congressional hearings on claims by tobacco companies that smoking was not addictive.

William Novelli, president of the National Centre for Tobacco-Free Kids, said the admission last month by the Liggett Group that smoking was addictive and could be harmful demonstrated the need for new hearings.

He said exectives of seven major tobacco companies should be asked about their testimony, made under oath at a 1994 House hearing, that smoking was not addictive and did not cause cancer. They also testified that their companies did not market cigarettes to children.

"It is clear that the chief executive officers who testified before Congress three years ago lied, but Congress has remained virtually silent about this fact. Americans deserve the truth," Novelli said in letter to the leaders of the House and Senate.

Separately, a senator and two House members said they would introduce legislation Tuesday to require tobacco companies to list all their ingredients, including any carcinogens, on cigarette packs, and to strengthen and increase the size of warning labels on packs.

Sen. Frank Lautenberg, a New Jersey Democrat, called the measure "the bill the industry fears the most." The bill was also co-sponsored by Reps. Marty Meehan, a Massachusetts Democrat, and James Hansen, a Republican from Utah.

Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat who questioned the tobacco executives when he was a House member, also called for new hearings. "It's time for Congress to bring the tobacco CEO's back and swear them in," Wyden said at a news conference with Novelli.
The Justice Department is investigating whether the executives committed perjury at the hearing and whether tobacco companies withheld information and lied to federal agencies.

Novelli's group is a coalition of over 100 organisations, including The American Medical Association, the American Cancer Society and the National Parent-Teachers Association. It is placing advertisements calling for hearings in several leading newspapers.

Liggett made the admissions as part of a settlement with 22 state attorneys general who have sued the tobacco industry to recoup the Medicaid health care costs of smoking. Liggett is owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd.
